lead: A power divider takes one microwave input and gives two or more outputs at a set power ratio. An attenuator lowers power by a known number of decibels. Both parts let a designer set signal level without guessing: the divider sets how power is shared, the attenuator sets how much reaches the next stage. They appear in antenna feeds, receiver front ends, test benches and phased arrays. The key ideas are matched ports, isolation between outputs, and adding decibels through a chain. Splits and losses are ratios of power, so count them in decibels of power, not in decibels of voltage.
prereq: You need: S-parameters for port waves and waveguide tees for the basic tee split.

blocks.text: A T-junction is a three-port made by joining three lines or waveguides. The input power P<sub>1</sub> splits between two arms. An ideal tee is lossless: output powers add to input power when reflections are absent. A simple tee is cheap and small, so it is used for rough splits and monitors.

A lossless reciprocal three-port cannot be matched at all three ports at once. A tee therefore reflects some power when its outputs are matched. It is not the best choice when a clean 50 Ω match matters.

A resistive divider uses three resistors in a star or delta. It can be matched at every port, but resistors turn part of the input into heat. For an equal two-way matched resistive divider, each output receives one quarter of input power: half is split and half is dissipated. That is 6.02 dB loss to each output.

blocks.where: P<sub>1</sub> is input power in W; P<sub>2</sub> and P<sub>3</sub> are output powers in W for an equal matched resistive divider. In dB, 10 log<sub>10</sub>(4) = 6.02 dB.

blocks.text: The Wilkinson divider is a three-port that uses two quarter-wave branches of impedance √2 Z<sub>0</sub> for an equal split between Z<sub>0</sub> ports. Z<sub>0</sub> is the system impedance, often 50 Ω. A resistor of 2Z<sub>0</sub> connects the two outputs.

At the design frequency, the quarter-wave lines and resistor make all three ports matched. The two outputs are isolated: a signal entering output 2 does not reach output 3. In ideal matched use the resistor carries no current, so the divider is lossless and each output gets half power, −3.01 dB.

blocks.where: S<sub>21</sub> and S<sub>31</sub> are voltage-wave transmission coefficients from input to outputs; S<sub>23</sub> is output-to-output isolation. |S|<sup>2</sup> is a power ratio.

blocks.text: Unequal split uses different branch impedances and a different resistor value. The bigger output receives more power. Bandwidth is limited because the branches are quarter-wave only near the design frequency. If an output is mismatched, reflected power is absorbed in the isolation resistor, so the divider is no longer lossless.

An attenuator reduces power by a fixed or adjustable number of decibels. A fixed pad is a resistor network, often T or π, chosen to present Z<sub>0</sub> at both ports. Common values are 3, 6, 10 and 20 dB. The pad absorbs the removed power as heat.

A step attenuator switches fixed pads in or out, so the loss changes in known steps, such as 1 dB. A variable attenuator changes continuously, using a potentiometer or a biased PIN diode. Pads match both ports, so they protect a source from a bad load and protect a load from a strong source.

blocks.where: A is attenuation in dB; P<sub>in</sub> and P<sub>out</sub> are powers in W. Cascaded pads add: A<sub>total</sub> = A<sub>1</sub> + A<sub>2</sub>. A level in dBm falls by A dB.

blocks.text: Power rating matters. A pad must dissipate P<sub>in</sub> − P<sub>out</sub>. A level of 20 dBm means 20 dB above 1 mW, that is 100 mW. A 6 dB pad leaves about 25.1 mW, so the pad heats by about 74.9 mW. Choose a rating above the input power, not just above the output power.

figure.caption: The Wilkinson splits the input equally through two quarter-wave branches. Notice the isolation resistor between the two outputs; it absorbs reflected power when an output is mismatched.

spec.aria: Wilkinson divider: input splits through two quarter-wave branches to two outputs, with an isolation resistor between the outputs.

examples.question: A 20 dBm source feeds a 6 dB fixed attenuator, then an ideal equal two-way Wilkinson divider with matched loads. Find the power at each output in dBm and in mW. Use a 3 dB split for the rounded answer and give the exact value too.
steps: dBm means decibels above 1 mW. Convert input: P<sub>in</sub> = 10<sup>20/10</sup> mW = 100 mW.
After the attenuator: A = 6 dB. P<sub>after</sub> = 100 × 10<sup>−6/10</sup> mW = 25.12 mW. Level = 20 − 6 = 14 dBm.
Exact half-power split: each output = 25.12/2 = 12.56 mW. Level = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(12.56/1 mW) = 10.99 dBm.
Rounded split loss: 14 − 3 = 11 dBm. Exact split loss is 3.01 dB, so 10.99 dBm is the precise value.
examples.answer: Each output is about 11 dBm (exact 10.99 dBm), or about 12.56 mW.
examples.check:
import math
pin_mw = 10 ** (20 / 10)
p_after_mw = pin_mw * 10 ** (-6 / 10)
p_each_mw = p_after_mw / 2
p_each_dbm = 10 * math.log10(p_each_mw)
p_round_dbm = 20 - 6 - 3
print(round(p_round_dbm, 2))
print(round(p_each_dbm, 2))
print(round(p_each_mw, 2))

traps: A 3 dB split is half power, not half voltage. Voltage falls by 1/√2; power falls by 1/2.
A Wilkinson is lossless only when all ports are matched. With a mismatched output, the isolation resistor turns reflected power into heat.
A matched pad is not a bare series resistor. It is designed to look like Z<sub>0</sub> at both ports; that match is its useful feature.
Do not add dBm values as if they were dB. 20 dBm minus 6 dB is 14 dBm; 20 dBm plus 20 dBm means 200 mW, not 40 dBm.
An equal matched resistive divider has about 6 dB loss to each output, not 3 dB, because half the power is dissipated in its resistors.

quiz.q: Define a power divider and an attenuator in one sentence each.
quiz.a: A power divider splits one input into two or more outputs at a set power ratio. An attenuator reduces power by a known number of decibels.

quiz.q: Why can a lossless reciprocal three-port not be matched at all three ports?
quiz.a: For a lossless reciprocal three-port, S<sup>†</sup>S = I with S<sub>11</sub> = S<sub>22</sub> = S<sub>33</sub> = 0 forces |S<sub>12</sub>||S<sub>13</sub>| = 0, |S<sub>12</sub>||S<sub>23</sub>| = 0, and |S<sub>13</sub>||S<sub>23</sub>| = 0. At least two of the three couplings must then be zero, which no real three-port tee satisfies, so all three ports cannot be matched at once.

quiz.q: A 10 dBm signal passes through a 3 dB pad, then an ideal equal Wilkinson divider. Find each output in dBm and mW.
quiz.a: Subtract the pad and the split: 10 − 3 − 3 = 4 dBm at each output. P = 10<sup>4/10</sup> mW = 2.51 mW.

quiz.q: One output of a Wilkinson is left open. What happens to the reflected power, and why is the other output still fairly isolated?
quiz.a: The open output reflects power. The isolation resistor absorbs much of that reflected power, so it does not all return to the input or reach the other output. The other output stays fairly isolated, though the match is not perfect away from the design frequency.

quiz.q: Write the dB formula for attenuation and the rule for cascaded pads.
quiz.a: A = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>) dB. Cascaded pads add: A<sub>total</sub> = A<sub>1</sub> + A<sub>2</sub>.

quiz.q: A 0 dBm signal goes through 10 dB and 6 dB pads in cascade. Find total attenuation and output power in mW.
quiz.a: Total attenuation = 10 + 6 = 16 dB. Output = 10<sup>−16/10</sup> mW = 0.0251 mW, or 25.1 µW.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wilkinson dividers appear in phased-array feed networks and MMIC power combiners, where unequal split and isolation matter. Digital step attenuators are common in test instruments and automatic gain control. RF pads are chosen by dB value and power rating, not by resistor size alone. Search next for Wilkinson unequal split design, PIN diode attenuator, and RF pad power rating.
